problem: Prior VLN data augmentation only works inside a scene. Speaker-generated paths (intra-scene augmentation, ISA) and EnvDrop's feature dropout (near-scene augmentation, NSA) do not explicitly reduce data bias across house scenes. Agents therefore overfit to the 61 seen R2R training scenes and generalize poorly to unseen ones.
motivation: R2R has only about 22K instruction-path pairs, while the space of possible paths grows exponentially with path length. The paper frames generalization through Vicinal Risk Minimization and assumes that augmented samples farther from the training distribution reduce generalization error more. It argues that inter-scene augmentation, which mixes two houses into a new cross-connected house, should beat intra-scene or near-scene augmentation at the same data size.
key_idea: Build new training environments by cutting two Matterport navigation graphs at a high-betweenness 'doorway' edge and cross-connecting them, with stitched panoramic views and orientation alignment. Fine-grained sub-path/sub-instruction alignments are then spliced into new instruction-path pairs that walk across both houses.
insight: Scene-level mixing gives more useful diversity than intra-scene path generation or feature noise. In the data-scaling ablation (reported only in a figure), REM beats both ISA (speaker-style) and NSA (EnvDrop-style) at matched instruction counts. Adding more mixed environments keeps helping, whereas adding more instructions from a fixed set of mixed environments saturates. Consistency between instruction and action is critical. Without orientation alignment, REM slightly hurts the IL+RL baseline on val-unseen (SR 46.0 vs 46.2), while with orientation alignment plus cross-viewpoint view replacement it reaches SR 48.6 / SPL 44.8. Replacing 3 of the 12 horizontal views at cross viewpoints is best; 4 views drops val-unseen SR to 47.9, so over-stitching the visuals hurts.
method: Key-vertex selection: compute vertex and edge betweenness centrality on each scene's navigation graph. Keep the top-10 vertices and top-10 edges, drop edges whose endpoints are not both among the top vertices, then pick the edge traversed by the most supervised training paths. Its two endpoints (v_s^key, v_t^key) are typically room entrances or corridors.

Cross-connected scene construction: randomly pair two training scenes, cut the key edges e^key1 and e^key2, and relink (v_s^key1, v_t^key2) and (v_s^key2, v_t^key1) to form a new graph G_C. 61 training scenes yield 116 mixed scenes.

Cross viewpoints (CCV): at each key viewpoint, splice the 12-way horizontal panorama. The 3 views around the direction of the next viewpoint are replaced with views from the other scene, so the observation features come from both houses.

Orientation alignment (OA): move v_t^key1, v_t^key2 and their attached vertices, swapping their positions, so the relative direction to the next viewpoint is preserved. Otherwise an instruction such as 'turn left' would no longer match the required action.

Cross path and instruction generation: use Fine-Grained R2R (FGR2R) sub-instruction/sub-path alignments to concatenate the sub-paths and sub-instructions before and after the key edge from the two scenes. This yields 5916 paths and 7022 instructions.
Training: merge the augmented triplets with the original training set (T_aug = T~ ∪ T) and train the baseline agents (IL+RL, EnvDrop, VLN↻BERT) with their original hyperparameters unchanged.

setting.backbone: Baseline agents retrained with REM data: EnvDrop-style LSTM seq2seq (IL+RL and EnvDrop) and VLN↻BERT (Recurrent VLN-BERT transformer); which VLN↻BERT initialization is used is not stated
setting.training_data: R2R train (61 scenes) plus REM-augmented data: 116 cross-connected scenes, 5916 paths, 7022 instructions, built with Fine-Grained R2R sub-instruction alignments. Baselines keep their original settings, presumably including their own augmented data (e.g., EnvDrop back-translation), though this is not stated. For R4R, the source of the REM data is not specified.

numbers_note: Baseline rows marked * are the authors' own reproductions, and REM's gains are measured against those rather than the published numbers. The claimed '+2.4 SPL over previous SOTA' matches reproduced VLN↻BERT test SPL 56.7; published VLN↻BERT is 57. The data-scaling comparison of REM vs ISA vs NSA appears only in a figure, with no numeric values. The orientation-alignment and view-count ablations (Tables 3-4) use only the IL+RL baseline on R2R val seen and unseen. The paper does not state how REM data were built for R4R.
results: REM improves all three baselines on R2R and R4R. VLN↻BERT+REM reaches 65.2 SR / 59.1 SPL on R2R test-unseen, versus 61.4 / 56.7 for the reproduced VLN↻BERT and 63 / 57 as published, making it the best entry in the table. It gets 63.6 / 57.9 on val-unseen. EnvDrop+REM improves test-unseen SR from 50.5 to 54.1 and SPL from 46.5 to 50.4 over reproduced EnvDrop. On R4R val-unseen, VLN↻BERT+REM gets SR 46.0, SPL 38.1, nDTW 46.3 and SDTW 22.7, beating EGP and BabyWalk on SR, nDTW and SDTW, but its CLS of 44.9 trails BabyWalk's 49.4.
limitations: The claim that REM shrinks the seen/unseen gap is not supported by the tables: the gap widens in absolute terms. For VLN↻BERT, SR goes from 70.7/61.4 to 75.4/63.6; for EnvDrop, from 64.4/51.1 to 70.1/53.8.

REM depends on fine-grained sub-instruction/sub-path alignments (FGR2R). It creates only one cut per scene, giving 116 mixed scenes. The stitched views at cross viewpoints come from different houses, and the resulting visual seams are handled heuristically (3 of 12 views replaced).
All results are single runs without variance. Gains over the published VLN↻BERT are small on val-unseen (+0.6 SR, +0.9 SPL), and the baselines are the authors' own reproductions.
